problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing **at least one number**) which has the largest sum, and return its sum.

A *subarray* is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements within an array. Note that you must take at least one element — even if every element is negative, you must return the largest single element rather than `0`.

**Follow-up:** if you have figured out the `O(N)` solution, try coding another solution using the *divide and conquer* approach, which is more subtle.
problems.real_world_analogy: Imagine your daily portfolio profit/loss for a year — some days gain, some lose. The Maximum Subarray is the best contiguous stretch of trading days: a run you cannot break in the middle, that, taken together, produced the highest cumulative profit. You must pick at least one day, even on a year where every day lost money (in which case you pick the smallest loss).

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum 6. Note that [4,-1,2,1,-5,4] sums to 5, which is worse — extending into the -5 hurts. The algorithm restarts whenever extending becomes worse than starting fresh.
Only one element; the only valid subarray is the array itself.
The entire array sums to 23. The single dip to -1 is more than recovered by the surrounding gains, so the optimal subarray is the whole array.
Every element is negative. Since we must take at least one, the answer is the largest single element, -1. A common bug is to initialize the running maximum to 0 — that returns 0 here, which is wrong.
The subarray [3,-2,5] sums to 6. Extending into -1 drops the sum to 5, so the algorithm stops there.

edge_cases: Single element (positive, negative, or zero) — answer is the element itself
All-negative array — answer is the maximum (least negative) element, not zero
All-positive array — answer is the sum of the entire array
Optimal subarray is at the very start or very end of the array
Optimal subarray is a single element flanked by larger negatives
Array length exactly 1 (boundary of the constraint)
hints: The brute force is to try every (i, j) pair and compute the sum directly. Can you avoid recomputing partial sums by accumulating as you extend the right endpoint?

For each ending index `i`, ask: what is the maximum sum of a subarray that ends *exactly* at `i`? Express this recursively in terms of the answer for `i-1` — you have only two choices: extend the previous best, or restart at `nums[i]`.

Let `f(i)` be the best subarray sum ending at index `i`. Then `f(i) = max(nums[i], f(i-1) + nums[i])`. The final answer is `max(f(0), f(1), ..., f(N-1))`. You don't need an array — just two scalars: the running `f(i-1)` and the global maximum so far. That's Kadane's Algorithm: O(N) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force (Running Sum)
approaches.summary: Enumerate every (i, j) subarray and track the maximum, accumulating the sum incrementally so each (i, j) costs O(1).
approaches.intuition:
Every contiguous subarray is uniquely determined by its left and right endpoints. The naïve naïve approach computes each subarray sum from scratch in O(N), giving O(N^3) total. We can do better by reusing work: as the right endpoint `j` advances by one with `i` fixed, the new sum is just the old sum plus `nums[j]`. That eliminates the inner sum computation and gives O(N^2).

This is still too slow for the constraint `N = 10^5` (would be 10^10 operations), but it's the right baseline to build intuition. Notice that for fixed `i`, the running sum either keeps growing or eventually becomes worse than restarting from a later index. That observation is the key to the optimal algorithm.
steps: Initialize `best` to negative infinity (NOT zero — must handle all-negative arrays).

approaches.name: Kadane's Algorithm (Optimal)
approaches.summary: One pass. At each index, decide to extend the previous best subarray or restart fresh at the current element.
approaches.intuition:
Define `f(i)` = the maximum sum of a subarray that ends *precisely at index `i`*. There are exactly two candidates:

- **Extend** the previous best ending at `i-1`: that gives `f(i-1) + nums[i]`.
- **Restart** at `i`: that gives just `nums[i]`.

We pick whichever is larger: `f(i) = max(nums[i], f(i-1) + nums[i])`. The final answer is `max(f(0), f(1), ..., f(N-1))` — we have to take the max over all ending positions because the best subarray could end anywhere.

Why is this correct? Any contiguous subarray ending at index `i` is either (a) just `[nums[i]]`, or (b) `[...something..., nums[i]]` where the prefix is itself a contiguous subarray ending at `i-1`. The best prefix to attach is by definition `f(i-1)`. If `f(i-1)` is negative, attaching it can only hurt, so we restart — that's exactly what the `max` selects.

**Space optimization:** we don't need the full `f` array — only `f(i-1)` (the running 'current') and the running global maximum 'best'. Two scalars, O(1) space.

The negative-only edge case is handled automatically: `best` is initialized to `nums[0]`, so even an all-negative input returns the largest element.
steps: Set `current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i])` — extend or restart.
Set `best = max(best, current)` — update the global maximum.
